paragraphs.text: The World Health Organization divides thy roid neoplasms into thyroid carcinomas, thyroid adenomas, and other thyroid tumors [1]. In this chapter, we will review thyroid nodules (TN), differentiated thyroid cancers (DTC; papillary thyroid cancer, PTC; follic ular thyroid cancer, FTC), and medullary thyroid cancer (MTC). The latter is usually associated with multiple endocrine neopla sia (MEN) type 2 in children [2]. Much has been learned about pediatric thyroid tumors since this material was last published, includ ing publication of the inaugural guidelines
paragraphs.heading: 18.1 Background

paragraphs.text: for the management of thyroid nodules and cancers in children [3]. This chapter will focus on recent updates in the field and includes a case study that demonstrates application of the 2015 Guidelines to patient care.

Thyroid nodules (TN) are discrete lesions that are distinct from the surrounding thyroid. Non-palpable TN may be found during imag ing for other reasons (“incidentalomas”) but have the same risk for differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC) as do palpable TN of similar size [3]. Estimates from ultrasound (US) and postmortem examination suggest that 0.2–5% of children and 13% of adolescents have thy roid nodules [4], and thyroid cysts occur in 57% of children screened using US [5]. However, it remains unclear how many of these lesions would ever grow to reach a threshold for clinical detection or require treatment. Factors that increase the risk for TN to develop in children include family his tory of TN or thyroid cancer, iodine defi ciency, radiation exposure, autoimmune thyroid disease (AITD), and several genetic syndromes.
paragraphs.heading: 18.2 Thyroid Nodules

paragraphs.text: The management of children with TN has changed over the past few decades. Prior to the 1980s, virtually all TN in children were removed. By the 1990s, high-resolution US and fine needle aspiration (FNA) were per formed to identify DTC preoperatively so that an appropriate “cancer surgery” could be per formed. Now, US and FNA are used to iden tify DTC and to diagnose benign TN. Similar to adults, up to 35% of TN will have indeter minate cytology [6]. Comprehensive nextgeneration sequencing panels analyzing for somatic oncogenic alterations can further inform the management of pediatric thyroid nodules [7, 8]; however, even with these advances there is a higher surgical resection rate for TN with benign and indeterminate cytology compared to adults [9].
paragraphs.heading: 18.2 Thyroid Nodules

paragraphs.text: In adults, 7–15% of TN are malignant, but the risk for DTC in children is higher (range 3–70%, average between 22% and 26%) [10]. The 2015 American Thyroid Association (ATA) Guidelines for Managing Thyroid Nodules and Cancer in Children suggest that palpation of the thyroid by experienced exam iners is sufficient screening to identify TN that require evaluation and treatment [3]. For patients at increased risk for developing TN and thyroid cancer, controversy continues to exist whether US screening should be used rather than palpation in an effort to detect PTC prior to LN metastasis [11, 12].
paragraphs.heading: Nodules

paragraphs.text: A detailed history of familial thyroid disor ders, iodine intake, radiation exposure, and antecedent thyroid disease should be obtained. The risk for DTC is 2.5-fold higher for chil dren with a family history of benign thyroid disease and fourfold higher for children with a family history of DTC [13]. US surveillance of at-risk children detects DTC of smaller size and with a lower incidence of lymph node metastasis (23.2% vs. 65.6%) and extrathyroi dal extension (20.9% vs. 56.2%), suggesting that US screening of children with a family history of thyroid cancer may offer benefit [14].
paragraphs.heading: Medical History

paragraphs.text: In addition, there are several specific genetic syndromes that are associated with TN and DTC. Benign and malignant thyroid tumors can occur in patients with PTEN [phosphatase and tensin homolog] Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome [PHTS; Cowden syndrome; Bannayan-Riley- Ruvalcaba Syndrome] [15, 16], DICER1 syn drome [17–19], familial adenomatous polyposis [FAP] [20, 21], and Carney complex [22]. With uncommon exception, the majority of DTC-associated tumor syndromes, includ ing PHTS, DICER1, and FAP, have lowinvasive behavior with a low risk for regional and distant metastasis. The exception is for
paragraphs.heading: Medical History

paragraphs.text: DICER1 where poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma and thyroblastoma have been reported, both associated with an increased risk for metastasis [23–25].
paragraphs.heading: Medical History

paragraphs.text: For pediatric patients diagnosed with MTC, MEN2 is the associated tumor predis position syndrome, diagnosed in 75% or more patients [2]. All of the thyroid tumor predis position syndromes followed an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance, with varying penetrance and expressivity for TN and thy roid cancer.
paragraphs.heading: Medical History

paragraphs.text: Chronic iodine deficiency and excess are asso ciated with an increased risk of thyroid dys function, thyroid nodules, and DTC [26, 27]. Up to one in three children worldwide are at risk for iodine deficiency [28]. In the United States, iodine deficiency in children is not well reported, but mild to moderate iodine defi ciency is common secondary to changes in dietary practices (increase in vegetarianism, decreased intake of dairy, use of sea salt and other) and changes in agricultural and manu facturing processes [29].
paragraphs.heading: 18.2.1.2 Iodine Intake

paragraphs.text: TN develop in childhood cancer survivors who received radiation therapy (RT) with exposure to the thyroid at a rate of about 2% annually and reach a peak incidence after 15–25 years [30–32]. The risk is greatest fol lowing RT at younger age and with doses up to 20–29 Gy [33–35]. Previous studies have demonstrated a linear dose–response relation ship between dosage of radiation and inci dence of secondary thyroid cancer [36]. Up to 20% of long-term cancer survivors have a TN > 1 cm detected by US that may not be apparent on physical exam [37]. The risk for DTC is increased in survivors who had Hodgkin lymphoma, leukemia, or central ner vous system tumors [38]. There is also a five fold greater risk following treatment for neuroblastoma, suggesting the possibility of shared genetic risk factors [39]. The optimal screening method for secondary DTC in childhood cancer survivors continues to be
paragraphs.heading: 18.2.1.3 Radiation Exposure

paragraphs.text: debated, with some favoring thyroid US for earlier detection of radiation-induced PTC while others recommending palpation to miti gate unnecesary procedures and survivor anx iety [12]. At medical centers with experience in performing and interpreting pediatric thyroid ultrasound, annual US surveillance should be initiated within 3 years of RT in patients <10 years at the time of exposure in an effort to identify PTC prior to widespread regional and distant metastasis.
paragraphs.heading: 18.2.1.3 Radiation Exposure

paragraphs.text: AIT, Graves’ disease, and goiter are associated with an increased risk for TN and DTC in children [40]. In one prospective study, US identified TN in 31.5% of children with AIT. Only one-third of the nodules could be palpated and of the 11 patients diagnosed with PTC only 4 nodules could be palpated [41]. In a retrospective review of patients referred for thyroidectomy, Kovatch et al. identified TN in 41% and DTC in 22% of chil dren and adolescents with Graves’ disease [42]. Lee et al. evaluated 113 Korean children with goiter and found nodules in 63.7% [43]. The prevalence of nodules in this cohort was much greater than that of a previous US cohort (17%), suggesting there may be regional, genetic, or environmental confound ers [44]. The 2015 ATA Guidelines recom mend an US should be performed whenever the gland feels suspicious or if abnormal lymphadenopathy is found on physical exami nation [3]. With the increased risk for DTC in patients with AIT and thyroid nodules, US should be performed to optimize the decision between radioiodine ablation versus thyroid ectomy for patients pursuing definitive treat ment of GD.

paragraphs.text: Children with suppressed TSH are more likely to have a hyperfunctioning (hot) TN with a lower risk of malignancy [45, 46]. Based on this data, if the sonographic appearance of the nodule is low risk (such as mixed solid cys

For nodules with indeterminate sono graphic features (such as solid lesions), FNA should be performed prior to definitive treat ment [47].

paragraphs.text: The US should describe the TN composition (solid, cystic, or spongiform), echogenicity, shape margins, presence or absence of echo genic foci (microcalcifications), and presence or absence of suspicious cervical lymphade nopathy [48–50]. Widely invasive forms of PTC, both diffuse sclerosing variant PTC (dsvPTC) [51] and widely invasive or infiltra tive follicular variant PTC (inf-fvPTC) [52] are more common in pediatrics and young adults than in older adults. DsvPTC and inffvPTC do not present as a discrete TN but do have abundant punctate echogenic foci (PEF) associated with microcalcifications that are readily visualized on US. Both dsvPTC and inf-fvPTC present as diffuse enlargement of a thyroid lobe or the entire gland and, in con trast to autoimmune thyroiditis, both are associated with bulky cervical metastatic lymphadenopathy [53].

FNA should also be performed on suspicious lymph nodes in the lateral neck compartments to determine whether a lateral neck dissection is indicated and which cervical levels should undergo compartmental dissec tion ( Fig. 18.2) [49, 50, 54]. Thyroglobulin [Tg] measured from the FNA needle washout may add to diagnostic accuracy if the cytol ogy from the lymph node is indeterminate for metastatic disease [55]. This is required to confirm the presence of DTC and to have an accurate preoperative plan for whether a lateral neck lymph node dissection should be performed.

All FNA results are categorized according to The Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology (TBSRTC), with the most recent edition having a pediatric specific table similarly divided into six tiers but with a higher risk of malignancy in category four compared to adults [56]: 1. Nondiagnostic or unsatisfactory
2. Benign 3. Atypia of undetermined significance (AUS) 4. Follicular neoplasm (FN) 5. Suspicious for malignancy (SFM) 6. Malignant

18.1 The recommendation for and extent of surgery are based on the individual DTC risk, the sonographic appearance of the nodule and regional lymph nodes, the somatic onco genic driver (if available), the risks of surgery, and the tolerance for uncertainty in the patient and family.

For children with a TN showing nondiagnostic cytopathology (TBSRTC I), repeat FNA or surgical removal (lobectomy) is an option. With the use of thinner FNA needles (27 gauge), there is no need to wait 3–6 months between FNA procedures as a shorter biopsy interval, typically 6–8 weeks, is not associated with skewing the results to indeterminate or suspicious cytology [59]. For children with benign cytopathology (TBSRTC II), followup is warranted. Surgery or non-surgical abla tive techniques, including radiofrequency or thermal ablation, may be considered for growth, compressive symptoms, or patient/ parent choice [60, 61].

In children with AUS (TBSRTC III), repeat FNA or review by a high-volume cyto pathologist may yield a definitive diagnosis, but up to 45% of AUS remain during repeat examination [58]. Molecular testing using comprehensive next-generation sequencing panels may aid in the diagnosis of AUS cytol ogy. Identification of a pathogenic variant in a gene associated with PTC (BRAF V600E, RET fusion, or NTRK fusion) is virtually diagnostic of PTC, which may avoid repeat FNA procedures and indicate total thyroidec tomy rather than diagnostic lobectomy [62,

63]. Identification of oncogenic variants asso ciated with either malignant or benign neo plasia (RAS, PTEN, or DICER1) [64] may not alter management; however, in the pres ence of reassuring sonographic features (com plex or solid composition with smooth margins, and no evidence of regional lymph node metastasis), the majority of DTC with these oncogenic driver alterations are associ ated with a low-risk for extrathyroidal disease [8] where lobectomy would be appropriate with further management based on the histo logic features of the nodule. Minimal and incomplete data exist to determine the reli ability of negative molecular testing results for excluding malignancy in children and ado lescents [65].

In children with FN cytology (TBSRTC IV), there appears to be approximately a 40–71% risk for DTC [57, 58]. Lobectomy has been the standard of care; however, similar to nodules with AUS cytology, somatic onco gene testing is being utilized to further inform DTC risk and management. TN lacking known mutations still carry a substantial DTC risk, and therefore, diagnostic lobec tomy continues to be recommended for all children with FN cytology. Total thyroidec tomy should be considered if the US is highly suspicious or if there are bilateral TN.
For children with FNA showing either SFM (TBSRTC V) or malignant (TBSRTC

VI) cytopathology, the risk for DTC is near 100% [56, 57]. For this reason, total thyroidec tomy ± central neck dissection is recom mended [3]. The goal of performing a prophylactic central neck dissection is to define the invasive behavior of the cancer in order to stratify the use of radioactive iodine based on the ATA pediatric risk levels [3]. The surgical risks of total thyroidectomy are greater than those for lobectomy but are reduced if the surgery is performed by a highvolume thyroid surgeon (who performs at least 25 or more thyroid surgeries annually) [66, 67]. Total thyroidectomy requires lifelong thyroid hormone replacement with levothy roxine (LT4), while thyroid lobectomy usually does not require LT4 replacement [68].

Only 1.8% of thyroid cancers develop in chil dren and adolescents, but the incidence has increased 2.3-fold over the last 40 years [69]. This increase cannot be entirely explained by detection of small, incidental lesions during unrelated imaging as the incidence of both intrathyroidal as well as thyroid cancer with regional and distant metastasis has increased over the same time frame [70]. Within pediat rics, DTC is the second most common cancer
paragraphs.heading: Cancers

paragraphs.text: of adolescent girls [71]. Adolescents have a tenfold greater incidence of DTC with a female/male preponderance (5:1) within this age group. Estimates from the SEER database report 5-year survival of 99.8% for children and adolescents with DTC confined to the thyroid and 97.1% for those with metastasis to regional lymph nodes [72]. For patients with intrathyroidal cancer and metastases limited to the cervical neck, overall remission rates are relatively high [73]. However, for patients with distant metastases, most often to the lungs, remission rates are low [74–77].
paragraphs.heading: Cancers

paragraphs.text: The treatment of children with DTC has evolved over time. In 1934, Schreiner and Murphy described DTC in children as a “fatal disease with few exceptions” [78]. Radioactive iodine (RAI) first came into use to treat DTC in 1946 [79]. In the 1980s, chil dren with DTC were sent for total thyroidec tomy but without preoperative staging, and lymph node dissection generally consisted of palpation to identify suspicious nodes that were removed by “berry picking,” leaving many with persistent disease. Essentially all children received RAI ablation, and the end point for treatment was to achieve no evi dence of disease (NED) based upon a nega tive RAI scan. Such treatment was effective, but was associated with a high risk for com plications and a risk of second malignancies. This high rate of complications and second malignancies along with other important dif ferences between DTC in children and adults prompted the creation of pediatric-specific treatment guidelines [3].
paragraphs.heading: Cancers

paragraphs.text: The major clinical differences between pediatric and adult DTC are: 1. TN are more likely to be malignant in chil

paragraphs.text: dren than in adults. 2. Children with PTC are more likely to have
paragraphs.heading: Cancers

paragraphs.text: regional lymph node involvement, extra thyroidal extension, and pulmonary metastases. 3. Children are less likely to die from disease
(2% long-term cause-specific mortality). 4. Many children with pulmonary metastases
(up to 93%) do not achieve remission; however, the majority develop stable, per sistent disease.

Long-term follow-up studies indicate that children with DTC have an increase in mor tality attributed to second malignancies that appear to be possibly related to the use of radiation and/or RAI [80]. For these reasons, the ATA Pediatric Guidelines suggest that the use of RAI should be stratified, limited to patients at risk for persistent, postsurgical dis ease and that the end point of therapy may not require NED in select patients, most nota bly patients categorized as ATA low-risk [3].

Fusion oncogenes (RET, NTRK, ALK, and BRAF) are more common in pubertal children and associated with an increased risk for regional LN and distant metastasis and BRAF V600E muta tions are more common in pubertal patients and associated with an increased risk for regional LN metastasis. Oncogenic altera tions associated with a lower risk for metasta sis (PTEN, DICER1, and RAS) are found across all pediatric age groups [8, 82].

paragraphs.text: There are six or more different forms of PTC with different variants correlating with somatic oncogenic alterations and invasive behavior. Classic (cPTC), solid (sPTC), dsvPTC, and inf-fvPTC are associated with a 50% or higher risk for LN metastases and most commonly associated with BRAF V600E
paragraphs.heading: (PTC)

paragraphs.text: (cPTC and sPTC) as well as fusion oncogenes (dsvPTC and inf-fvPTC) [1]. For patients with lateral neck LN metastases, there is a 15–20% risk for distant metastases, most commonly to the lungs [77]. In contrast, follicular variant PTC (fvPTC), in particular the invasiveencapsulated type (Ienc-fvPTC), have a lower risk for LN and distant metastases with RAS and DICER1 mutations and PAX8-PPARgamma fusions more common in Ienc-fvPTC and the BRAF V600E mutation being more common in inv-fvPTC [52, 83, 84].

paragraphs.text: Total or near-total thyroidectomy (TT) is recommended for the majority of chil dren with TBSRTC category V or VI. Recurrence risks are tenfold greater if less extensive surgery is performed and three fold greater if inadequate lymph node dis section is performed [87, 88]. In both procedures, the left and right thyroid lobes, the pyramidal lobe (when present), and the isthmus are resected. However, in near-TT,

paragraphs.text: a small amount of thyroid tissue (<1–2%) is frequently left at the entry of the recur rent laryngeal nerve (RLN) and/or supe rior parathyroids in an effort to decrease the risk of complications. TT is recom mended because children frequently have bilateral (38%) disease [89, 90] with an increased risk for recurrence when less extensive surgery is performed [91].

paragraphs.text: 18.1 18.4 All lymph node dissections should be compartment-based because recurrence rates are higher when “berry picking” is performed [97]. Although TT and central neck dissection (CND) are associated with greater risks of hypoparathyroidism and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury [98], the risks are minimized when surgery is per formed by a high-volume thyroid surgeon [66, 67, 99].
18.4 The two most common surgical com plications are recurrent laryngeal nerve

(RLN) damage and hypoparathyroidism. Damage to the RLN is associated with voice change secondary to injury to any of the external branches of the superior laryngeal nerves and/or the recurrent laryngeal nerves and can affect the strength, projection, and quality of the voice. Bilateral nerve injury may compro mise the airway with need for a tracheos tomy. With the availability and efficacy of RAI, as well as novel tyrosine kinase inhibitors, purposeful sacrifice of a RLN in an attempt to achieve surgical remission should be avoided. Careful visualization of all nerve branches and the use of elec trodes to identify and monitor nerve func tion during the procedure may help reduce
the risk of nerve injury [100, 101]. The risk of injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve should be less than 3% with total thyroid ectomy [102].

Due to their small size and delicate blood supply, ischemic injury to the para thyroid glands may also occur. The risk of permanent hypocalcemia is rare with lobectomy and up 7% with total thyroidec tomy in children in pediatric thyroid cen ters [102]. Using an intracapsular approach for TT reduces the risk of damaging the blood supply to the superior parathyroid glands [103]. If the parathyroid glands appear threatened during surgery, auto transplantation into a sternocleidomas toid muscle should be performed. Intra- or

perioperative parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels may help to identify those at greatest risk for postsurgical hypoparathyroidism [104, 105]. Postoperative hypocalcemia (occurring in up to 50% of patients) is treated with oral calcium and calcitriol. A low postoperative PTH predicts the need for treatment but does not predict the like lihood of permanent hypoparathyroidism [105]. 3. Stratification of RAI after initial surgery
1. ATA Pediatric Low Risk

Pediatric low-risk category includes disease grossly confined to the thyroid with no cervical lymph node disease (N0) or patients with <5 lymph nodes with metastatic disease from the central (level VI/VII) compartment (N1a) [94, 95, 106]. In patients that undergo lobectomy, uni lateral, multifocal disease does not appear to be a predictor of bilateral dis ease, especially in T1 tumors [95, 96]. A recent prospective study in adults [107] and a retrospective study in pediatrics confirm similarly excellent outcomes in
low-risk patients that do not receive RAI therapy [108]. 2. ATA Pediatric Intermediate Risk

Pediatric intermediate-risk category includes N1a disease with between 6 and 10 metastatic lymph nodes or unilateral, lateral neck metastasis (N1b). The pres ence of extrathyroidal extension (micro scopic or gross) is also considered an intermediate risk for persistent postsurgi cal disease, especially if the initial surgery did not include a central neck lymph node dissection (CND) [106, 109]. 3. ATA Pediatric High Risk
Pediatric high-risk category includes >10 metastatic lymph nodes, bilateral lat eral neck metastasis (N1b), or distant

metastasis (M1) [106]. Patients in this group are at the highest risk for persistent postsurgical disease, including distant metastasis. For ATA pediatric intermedi ate- and high-risk patients, a TSHstimulated Tg and diagnostic RAI whole body scan (DxWBS) are recommended to determine if treatment with 131Iodine is warranted.

In patients without TgAb, the TSH-stimulated Tg (TSH > 30 mIU/L) is a reliable marker for evaluating persistent, residual disease with a TSH-stimulated Tg < 2 ng/mL having a 94.9% predictive value for the absence of persistent disease [110]. In TgAb-positive patients, the presence of TgAb alone cannot be interpreted

as a sign of persistent disease with a greater need for reliance on radiologic and RAI-WBS imaging. RAI therapy may be avoided in TgAb-negative patients if the TSH-stimulated Tg is undetectable and there is no evidence of RAI activity on the DxWBS. There is an increased likelihood for distant metastasis in pediatric patients with a TSH-stimulated Tg of >156 ng/mL [111].

For patients where RAI is deemed to be beneficial, the TSH must be above 30 mIU/L to facilitate uptake. This can be induced by ~14 days of thyroid hormone withdrawal [112]. Alternately, recombinant human TSH (rhTSH) can be used for remnant ablation with RAI in low-risk patients; however, there are no studies confirming the effectiveness of this strategy for the treatment of persistent regional and distant metastasis in children [113]. A low-iodine diet is prescribed for 2 weeks prior to therapy (see www.thyca. org and www.lidlifecommunity.org). For children who received intravenous contrast during CT during the preoperative evalua tion, it is not necessary to delay RAI-WBS as long as it is 6–8 weeks after exposure to the iodinated contrast and the patient completes a low-iodine diet for 2 weeks prior to the WBS and potential 131I therapy. A 24-h urine iodine prior to administering RAI therapy can be considered if there is any concern with the goal <50 mg/24 h.

Selection of the administered activity (dose) of RAI is based on a number of fac tors, most importantly the Tg level as well as the location and amount of RAI avid disease on DxWBS. The initial extent of disease inva siveness should also be considered. In select ing the delivered 131I activity, some adjust 131I dose according to weight or body surface area (BSA) and give a fraction (e.g., child’s weight in kg/70 kg) based on the typical adult dose used to treat similar disease extent. Others suggest that 131I doses should be based entirely on body weight, with a general approach for typical 131I dosing for patients with persistent disease being 0.5–1.0 mCi/kg (max dose of 30–50 mCi) for thyroid bed/central neck activ ity, 1.0–1.5 mCi/kg (max dose 100 mCi) for lateral neck activity, and 1.5–2.5 mCi/kg (max dose 150 mCi) for pulmonary activity [3].

Dosimetry may be used to limit lung reten tion to <80 mCi at 48 h and blood/bone mar row exposure to <200 cGy and is useful in small children, children with diffuse lung uptake or significant distant metastases, chil dren who received chemotherapy or radiation therapy for other malignancies, and those undergoing multiple treatments. Lesional dosimetry can be performed in children with substantial lung involvement or large tumor burden at other sites, such as bone [114]. For patients that receive RAI therapy, a posttreat ment scan should be obtained 5–8 days after all RAI treatments [3]. For both the Dx and the post-RAI treatment WBS, the addition of SPECT/CT should be considered to clarify the anatomic location of metastatic disease if the information from the WBS is inadequate.

For patients that receive RAI therapy, a post-RAI treatment WBS (RxWBS) should be performed approximately 5–7 days after RAI therapy with up to 15% of scans showing a new area of uptake compared to the DxWBS secondary to increased sensitivity associated with a higher delivered RAI dose. Singlephoton emission computed tomography with integrated CT (SPECT-CT) should be com bined with the DxWBS or the post-RAI treat ment (RxWBS) to confirm RAI uptake in an unexpected location [115]. For patients with persistent lateral neck lymph node disease noted on the DxWBS, surgical dissection should be completed prior to RAI therapy, especially if there are multiple LNs > 1 cm in size [116].

18.6 Response to the initial treatment is divided into the following categories; (1) excellent response, (2) biochemical incomplete response, (3) structural incomplete response, or (4) indeterminate response, collectively called dynamic risk stratification (DRS) [108].
paragraphs.heading: Stratification and Management

paragraphs.text: The goal of DRS is to define remission and to determine if and when additional therapy is warranted based on biochemical (Tg and TgAb) and radiological data. In general, bio chemical data (TSH, Tg and TgAb) are fol lowed every 3–6 months and radiological imaging every 6 months, both with decreasing frequency if the data are reassuring for remis sion. Neck US is the first line for radiologic surveillance of the neck and non-contrast chest CT is the optimal radiological modality to follow patients with pulmonary metastasis. For a disease with slow growth, patience is an important path to pursue. This is highlighted by data showing that structural and biochemi cal response to initial RAI therapy may not be reached for up to 15–24 months, or longer, after treatment [117, 118].

paragraphs.text: Thyroglobulin may be measured using immunometric assays (IMA), radioimmuno assay (RIA), or by liquid chromatography dual-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Ultrasensitive assays have a lower detection limit of <0.1 ng/mL and are preferred to fol low disease status in patients with DTC [119]. Approximately 20–25% of patients will have an elevated TgAb titer that may interfere with accurate assessment of Tg levels. TgAb inter ference with IMA assays is the most signifi cant and almost always results in underestimation of Tg (i.e., a potentially false-negative test). In the majority of com mercial laboratories, if a Tg/TgAb panel is ordered, the lab will screen for TgAb and if elevated will run Tg by radioimmunoassay (RIA) or LC-MS/MS secondary to more accurate and reliable performance compared to IMA [119]. As a general rule, all specimens sent for Tg measurement in DTC patients require concomitant TgAb testing because TgAb status can change over time and even very low TgAb concentrations can interfere with assessment of disease status.

Radioactive iodine therapy does not appear to provide any benefit in regard to outcome for ATA pediatric low-risk patients and its use should be limited. Initial postoperative staging includes a TSH-suppressed serum thyroglobulin (Tg) with the interpretation of serum Tg based not only on the magnitude of serum Tg but its trend over time. Children who have undergone total thyroidectomy by an experienced thyroid surgeon may have an undetectable TSH-suppressed Tg within 6–12 months from surgery [108]. For this group of patients, neck US is adequate to surveil for anatomic disease, initially every 6 months extending to annually once remission is achieved. Remission is defined by an undetectable Tg and no evidence of anatomic disease on neck ultrasound.

In these patients, if the TgAb is rising over time, radiological investigation with neck US and chest CT, followed by DxWBS if negative, should be pursued in an effort to find an explanation [123] ( Fig. 18.6). For patients that have undergone lobec tomy, US is the best modality to surveil for persistent or recurrent disease as the remaining health thyroid tissue continues to produce Tg. 2. Risk

Similar to ATA low-risk patients, cervical neck US is the mainstay for surveillance with assess ment of all levels of the neck critical to assess for persistent or recurrent disease. Excellent response in these risk categories is defined as an undetectable unstimulated Tg (obtained during TSH suppression) as well as neck US and, if applicable, distant anatomic imaging, most commonly chest CT without IV con trast. A TSH-stimulated Tg with a DxWBS may be considered in high-risk patients, but with broad availability of ultrasensitive Tg assays, this may not be a necessary procedure to define excellent response [119].

For patients found to have with persistent, cervical neck structural disease, repeat surgery should be considered rather than repeat RAI therapy. This is especially true if there are lymph nodes larger than 1 cm in size where RAI is less effective in achieving [116, 124]. In select patients, non-surgical chemical, ther mal, or radio-frequency ablation may be con sidered depending on local expertise [125–127]. If repeat surgery is considered, US-guided methylene-blue labeling prior to skin incision may aid the surgeon in finding the persistent disease.

In patients with pulmonary metastasis (M1), a limited number will achieve remission with RAI therapy. The exception where one RAI treatment may be adequate is in patients with pulmonary metastasis only noted on the initial WBS without anatomic correlation on dedicated chest CT [75]. For patients with anatomically detectable disease by dedicated

chest CT, a portion may achieve remission with repeated RAI dosing, however, some of these patients may demonstrate stable, persis tent disease with low disease-specific mortal ity and repeat RAI therapy is associated with an increased risk for RAI-induced pulmonary fibrosis [128, 129]. For patients with persistent pulmonary metastasis, some may progress decades after initial treatment with one large study reporting progression-free survival of 76% at 5 years, decreasing to 66% at 10 years from diagnosis [130]. A decision to give repeat dosing must be individualized based on ana tomic response after a typical observation period of 12 months or longer between dosing to fully assess the previous RAI treatment. More recent, contemporary data from multi ple institutes reports a low-likelihood of pedi atric patients with pulmonary metastasis achieving an excellent response even after multiple courses of RAI with an associated increased risk for pulmonary fibrosis as well as disease-specific mortality [74–76, 131].

A small percent of patients will develop anatomic progression, termed RAI-refractory disease, defined as [132, 133]: 1. Absence of RAI uptake in metastases 2. 131I uptake is present in some but not other
tumor foci 3. DTC metastasis progress despite 131I uptake 4. Progressive disease despite receiving a
cumulative dose of 131I > 600 mCi (adult data)

These patients should be considered for tyro sine-kinase inhibitory or oncogene-specific inhibitory therapy in consultation with a pedi atric oncologist with experience in treating pediatric patients with advanced, progressive thyroid cancer [134, 135]. Several of the drugs are associated with resensitization or enhanced sensitization to RAI with on-going research exploring if repeat RAI, post-systemic ther apy, is associated with increased efficacy and remission [136, 137].
As previously mentioned, children with diffuse pulmonary metastases and high RAI uptake in the lung are at risk for treatmentinduced pulmonary fibrosis. In these cases,

lower single and cumulative 131Iodine activi ties may help limit radiation exposure to the adjacent normal lung parenchyma [114]. Serial chest CT every 6 months should be uti lized to determine the effect of RAI therapy on the lung metastasis as well as the surveil for potential development of pulmonary fibrosis. In general, pulmonary function testing (PFT) in children with lung metastases is not an effective tool to surveil for pulmonary metas tasis; however, PFTs should be considered for patients with pulmonary metastasis that develop non-exertional tachypnea with or without hypoxia.

In conjunction with radiological imaging, the serum Tg is a critical component in the man agement of DTC, both at the initial postop erative staging and during long-term surveillance. At the same degree of TSH suppression, the Tg level obtained while the patient is on levothyroxine is thought to be the best predictor of changes in tumor mass [3, 119]. Therefore, monitoring of the TSHsuppressed Tg along with radiological moni toring is the ideal approach to detect recurrence or disease progression.

In ATA pediatric low risk patients, an unstimulated Tg defines biochemical remis sion. In ATA pediatric intermediate and high risk patients, a stimulated Tg may be consid ered to confirm remission based on studies reporting that an undetectable Tg on levothy roxine therapy may not always predict an undetectable TSH-stimulated Tg [138–140]. A minimally elevated Tg (<10 ng/mL) in chil dren should not automatically result in addi tional therapy unless there is other evidence for active disease, either anatomic localization of disease on radiological imaging or an increasing trend in serum Tg over at least 1 year of surveillance. Patients with DTC can have a continual decline in Tg over many years without additional therapy [118].

An increase in serum Tg assessed with sim ilar TSH levels indicates that progressive dis ease is likely. Restaging and appropriate treatment, whether medical (RAI or systemic therapy) and/or surgery, is based on the degree

of Tg elevation, the trend in Tg over time, and the results of radiological studies. When imag ing fails to confirm disease, the clinical impor tance of a low-level disease burden identified only by Tg in children is not clear, and there is no absolute serum Tg value above which empiric treatment is indicated.

paragraphs.text: Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) is a rare neuroendocrine malignancy that arises from the calcitonin-secreting, parafollicular C cells of the thyroid and comprises 5% or less of pediatric thyroid cancers per year [2]. Since it does not derive from the thyroid follicular epi thelium, MTC does not produce Tg or con centrate iodine and does not respond to TSH suppression or stimulation. However, MTC secretes calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), both of which serve as excel lent tumor markers that are utilized in screening of disease onset, assessment of dis ease burden, and monitoring for recurrence/ progression in patients with treated disease.
paragraphs.heading: Carcinoma (MTC)

paragraphs.text: 18.3 MTC is characterized by a predictable, stepwise progression from C-cell hyperplasia to noninvasive, microscopic MTC and ulti mately to invasive, metastatic disease to regional lymph nodes and distant sites, most commonly the lungs, liver, and bone [147]. Genetic testing for RET mutations has been incorporated into routine clinical care and has ushered in an era wherein children and young adults with MEN2 rarely present with clinical MTC, unless they are members of a newly

Thus, most children with MEN2 (with the notable excep tion of MEN2B; see below) will be diagnosed via identification of a pathogenic RET muta tion prior to development of CCH or MTC. In adults, most MTC cases are sporadic, associ ated with somatic mutations in RET and RAS [2].

paragraphs.heading: Neoplasia 2B

paragraphs.text: MEN2B is due to a de novo RET mutation in >90% of cases, and >95% of MEN2B patients will have the pathognomonic M918 T RET mutation. MEN2B mutations may also include double RET mutations involving codon 804 and the A883F mutation, which may be associated with less aggressive MTC [2, 150].
paragraphs.heading: Neoplasia 2B

paragraphs.text: After MTC metastasizes beyond the thyroid, it most often becomes an incurable disease that may ultimately shorten survival. Given our ability to diagnose MEN2 via predictive genetic testing, hereditary metastatic MTC is one of the malignancies that can be prevented via early thyroidectomy. When total thyroid ectomy is performed by an experienced sur geon prior to the onset of metastatic disease, children with MEN2 can achieve remission and have an excellent long-term outcome [152].
paragraphs.heading: in MEN2

paragraphs.text: At the time of total thyroidectomy, a cen tral neck dissection is recommended for patients whose basal calcitonin is >40 pg/mL or for those in whom there is a clinical suspi cion for lymph node metastases. Contralateral neck dissection is considered if the basal serum calcitonin is >200 pg/mL and FNA of an ipsilateral lateral neck lymph node is posi tive [2, 148]. A preoperative serum calcitonin level >2000 pg/mL is associated with an increased risk for metastasis to the medias tum/lungs and >10,000 pg/mL to liver and bone [156].
paragraphs.heading: in MEN2

paragraphs.text: As discussed above, total thyroidec tomy ± central neck dissection remains the mainstay of treatment for MTC. The exact surgical approach depends on the specific RET mutation as well as the primary tumor size, the calcitonin level, and the extent of neck disease identified on preoperative neck ultrasound [2, 148, 150]. The goal of early sur gery is to remove the thyroid when the disease is at the c-cell hyperplasia or microscopic MTC state as this is associated with a high likelihood of remission. Remission in MEN2B
paragraphs.heading: in MEN2

paragraphs.text: is often unattainable due to the fact that most surgeries in this population are therapeutic (instead of prophylactic or early), an unfortu nate reality resulting from the delayed diagno sis of MEN2B in most cases [149, 151, 152].
paragraphs.heading: in MEN2

paragraphs.text: 18.3 When not diagnosed, and treated before the onset of metastatic disease, hereditary MTC is generally incurable yet may demon strate an indolent clinical course with stable disease over decades. A more aggressive clini cal course and poorer outcome can be pre dicted by a rapidly rising CEA out of proportion to calcitonin and a fast tumor marker doubling time [2]. For patients with a significant MTC burden and symptomatic or progressive metastatic disease, molecular tar geted therapies that inhibit RET or other receptor tyrosine kinases involved in angio genesis should be considered [159, 160]. These agents should also be considered for neoadju vant use (prior to surgery) in patients that present with widely invasive cervical neck dis ease where there is concern over an increased risk for surgical complications secondary to airway compromise, engulfment of the carotid sheath, or spread into the retrosternal com partment [134, 161].

The patient is placed on levothyroxine suppressive therapy with a plan to follow serum Tg levels every 3–6 months with repeat neck ultrasound and non-contrast chest CT

every 6 months with a plan to decrease the fre quency of surveillance if the data supports a trend toward remission. The family is coun seled that additional therapy may be neces sary as the current data suggests a very-low likelihood of remission for pediatric patients with pulmonary metastasis. For patients with stable, persistent disease, additional therapy may not be beneficial; however, for patients with progressive disease additional therapy, including incorporation of oncogene-specific inhibitory therapy, may be considered within the care of a high-volume pediatric thyroid center with expertise in using oncologic ther apy. The timing and type of additional ther apy will be determined based on the follow-up biochemical and anatomic radiological imag ing data.

There is an increased rate of malignancy for pediatric patients diagnosed with a thyroid nodule compared to an adult; however, the use of fine needle aspiration biopsy should be limited to nodules with indeterminate to higher risk sonographic features. For patients with differentiated thyroid cancer, the out come is excellent, but therapy must be indi vidualized in order to reduce the risk of treatment-associated complications. The approach to surgery should be stratified based on the ultrasound features, the cytology as well as the oncogenic driver (when available). For patients with unifocal nodules with inde terminate cytology, lobectomy should be con sidered. For patients with malignant cytology, total thyroidectomy is often pursued; how ever, lobectomy may be considered for patients with unifocal PTC without evidence of cervi cal neck lymph node metastasis. Data from the prophylactic, central neck lymph node dis section helps determine the invasive behavior of PTC and may be used to stratify comple tion thyroidectomy as well as radioiodine therapy, the later based on the ATA pediatric risk levels. Follow-up staging with Tg and TgAb levels, as well as radiological imaging, is used to assess response to therapy and iden tify children who may benefit from additional treatment. FTC in pediatrics is most com monly minimally invasive where lobectomy is adequate to achieve remission. In patients with angioinvasive FTC, long-term surveil lance is required as metastatic disease may not present for 5–10 years after initial surgery. MTC in pediatrics is most commonly associ ated with MEN2 with the timing of surgery and surveillance for associated pheochromo cytoma and hyperparathyroidism based on the specific germline codon mutation in the RET-protooncogene.

Patients with MEN2B should have thy roidectomy by 1 year of age. ### 18.1 Background The World Health Organization divides thy roid neoplasms into thyroid carcinomas, thyroid adenomas, and other thyroid tumors [1]. In this chapter, we will review thyroid nodules (TN), differentiated thyroid cancers (DTC; papillary thyroid cancer, PTC; follic ular thyroid cancer, FTC), and medullary thyroid cancer (MTC). The latter is usually associated with multiple endocrine neopla sia (MEN) type 2 in children [2]. Much has been learned about pediatric thyroid tumors since this material was last published, includ ing publication of the inaugural guidelines ### 18 for the management of thyroid nodules and cancers in children [3]. This chapter will focus on recent updates in the field and includes a case study that demonstrates application of the 2015 Guidelines to patient care. ### 18.2 Thyroid Nodules Thyroid nodules (TN) are discrete lesions that are distinct from the surrounding thyroid. Non-palpable TN may be found during imag ing for other reasons (“incidentalomas”) but have the same risk for differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC) as do palpable TN of similar size [3]. Estimates from ultrasound (US) and postmortem examination suggest that 0.2–5% of children and 13% of adolescents have thy roid nodules [4], and thyroid cysts occur in 57% of children screened using US [5]. However, it remains unclear how many of these lesions would ever grow to reach a threshold for clinical detection or require treatment. Factors that increase the risk for TN to develop in children include family his tory of TN or thyroid cancer, iodine defi ciency, radiation exposure, autoimmune thyroid disease (AITD), and several genetic syndromes. The management of children with TN has changed over the past few decades. Prior to the 1980s, virtually all TN in children were removed. By the 1990s, high-resolution US and fine needle aspiration (FNA) were per formed to identify DTC preoperatively so that an appropriate “cancer surgery” could be per formed. Now, US and FNA are used to iden tify DTC and to diagnose benign TN. Similar to adults, up to 35% of TN will have indeter minate cytology [6]. Comprehensive nextgeneration sequencing panels analyzing for somatic oncogenic alterations can further inform the management of pediatric thyroid nodules [7, 8]; however, even with these advances there is a higher surgical resection rate for TN with benign and indeterminate cytology compared to adults [9]. ## PDF page 455 | printed page 445 ### 18.2.1 Evaluation of Thyroid ### Nodules In adults, 7–15% of TN are malignant, but the risk for DTC in children is higher (range 3–70%, average between 22% and 26%) [10]. The 2015 American Thyroid Association (ATA) Guidelines for Managing Thyroid Nodules and Cancer in Children suggest that palpation of the thyroid by experienced exam iners is sufficient screening to identify TN that require evaluation and treatment [3]. For patients at increased risk for developing TN and thyroid cancer, controversy continues to exist whether US screening should be used rather than palpation in an effort to detect PTC prior to LN metastasis [11, 12]. ### 18.2.1.1 Family and Individual ### Medical History A detailed history of familial thyroid disor ders, iodine intake, radiation exposure, and antecedent thyroid disease should be obtained. The risk for DTC is 2.5-fold higher for chil dren with a family history of benign thyroid disease and fourfold higher for children with a family history of DTC [13]. US surveillance of at-risk children detects DTC of smaller size and with a lower incidence of lymph node metastasis (23.2% vs. 65.6%) and extrathyroi dal extension (20.9% vs. 56.2%), suggesting that US screening of children with a family history of thyroid cancer may offer benefit [14]. In addition, there are several specific genetic syndromes that are associated with TN and DTC. Benign and malignant thyroid tumors can occur in patients with PTEN [phosphatase and tensin homolog] Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome [PHTS; Cowden syndrome; Bannayan-Riley- Ruvalcaba Syndrome] [15, 16], DICER1 syn drome [17–19], familial adenomatous polyposis [FAP] [20, 21], and Carney complex [22]. With uncommon exception, the majority of DTC-associated tumor syndromes, includ ing PHTS, DICER1, and FAP, have lowinvasive behavior with a low risk for regional and distant metastasis. The exception is for DICER1 where poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma and thyroblastoma have been reported, both associated with an increased risk for metastasis [23–25]. For pediatric patients diagnosed with MTC, MEN2 is the associated tumor predis position syndrome, diagnosed in 75% or more patients [2]. All of the thyroid tumor predis position syndromes followed an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance, with varying penetrance and expressivity for TN and thy roid cancer. ### 18.2.1.2 Iodine Intake Chronic iodine deficiency and excess are asso ciated with an increased risk of thyroid dys function, thyroid nodules, and DTC [26, 27]. Up to one in three children worldwide are at risk for iodine deficiency [28]. In the United States, iodine deficiency in children is not well reported, but mild to moderate iodine defi ciency is common secondary to changes in dietary practices (increase in vegetarianism, decreased intake of dairy, use of sea salt and other) and changes in agricultural and manu facturing processes [29]. ### 18.2.1.3 Radiation Exposure TN develop in childhood cancer survivors who received radiation therapy (RT) with exposure to the thyroid at a rate of about 2% annually and reach a peak incidence after 15–25 years [30–32]. The risk is greatest fol lowing RT at younger age and with doses up to 20–29 Gy [33–35]. Previous studies have demonstrated a linear dose–response relation ship between dosage of radiation and inci dence of secondary thyroid cancer [36]. Up to 20% of long-term cancer survivors have a TN > 1 cm detected by US that may not be apparent on physical exam [37]. The risk for DTC is increased in survivors who had Hodgkin lymphoma, leukemia, or central ner vous system tumors [38]. There is also a five fold greater risk following treatment for neuroblastoma, suggesting the possibility of shared genetic risk factors [39]. The optimal screening method for secondary DTC in childhood cancer survivors continues to be ## PDF page 456 | printed page 446 debated, with some favoring thyroid US for earlier detection of radiation-induced PTC while others recommending palpation to miti gate unnecesary procedures and survivor anx iety [12]. At medical centers with experience in performing and interpreting pediatric thyroid ultrasound, annual US surveillance should be initiated within 3 years of RT in patients <10 years at the time of exposure in an effort to identify PTC prior to widespread regional and distant metastasis. ### 18.2.1.4 Autoimmune Thyroid ### Disease AIT, Graves’ disease, and goiter are associated with an increased risk for TN and DTC in children [40]. In one prospective study, US identified TN in 31.5% of children with AIT. Only one-third of the nodules could be palpated and of the 11 patients diagnosed with PTC only 4 nodules could be palpated [41]. In a retrospective review of patients referred for thyroidectomy, Kovatch et al. identified TN in 41% and DTC in 22% of chil dren and adolescents with Graves’ disease [42]. Lee et al. evaluated 113 Korean children with goiter and found nodules in 63.7% [43]. The prevalence of nodules in this cohort was much greater than that of a previous US cohort (17%), suggesting there may be regional, genetic, or environmental confound ers [44]. The 2015 ATA Guidelines recom mend an US should be performed whenever the gland feels suspicious or if abnormal lymphadenopathy is found on physical exami nation [3]. With the increased risk for DTC in patients with AIT and thyroid nodules, US should be performed to optimize the decision between radioiodine ablation versus thyroid ectomy for patients pursuing definitive treat ment of GD. ### 18 ### 18.2.1.5 A Serum Thyrotropin (TSH) ### Level Should Be Obtained Children with suppressed TSH are more likely to have a hyperfunctioning (hot) TN with a lower risk of malignancy [45, 46]. Based on this data, if the sonographic appearance of the nodule is low risk (such as mixed solid cys tic lesions with smooth margins and no evi dence of regional lymph node metastasis), definitive treatment with radioiodine ablation or lobectomy can be considered without FNA. For nodules with indeterminate sono graphic features (such as solid lesions), FNA should be performed prior to definitive treat ment [47]. ### 18.2.1.6 A Dedicated Thyroid ### and Neck US Should Be Performed on All Children with a Suspected or Incidental TN The US should describe the TN composition (solid, cystic, or spongiform), echogenicity, shape margins, presence or absence of echo genic foci (microcalcifications), and presence or absence of suspicious cervical lymphade nopathy [48–50]. Widely invasive forms of PTC, both diffuse sclerosing variant PTC (dsvPTC) [51] and widely invasive or infiltra tive follicular variant PTC (inf-fvPTC) [52] are more common in pediatrics and young adults than in older adults. DsvPTC and inffvPTC do not present as a discrete TN but do have abundant punctate echogenic foci (PEF) associated with microcalcifications that are readily visualized on US. Both dsvPTC and inf-fvPTC present as diffuse enlargement of a thyroid lobe or the entire gland and, in con trast to autoimmune thyroiditis, both are associated with bulky cervical metastatic lymphadenopathy [53]. ### 18.2.1.7 ### 18.1 18.2 18.1 ## PDF page 457 | printed page 447 ## PDF page 458 | printed page 448 nancy.
